list.listitem: Bartholin abscess (BA) is a common vulvar condition in women of reproductive age.
Patients typically present with a soft, painful, fluctuant lump 1 to 3 cm in diameter on either side of the labia . C
Culture of abscess fluid is recommended, but biopsy or imaging are not recommended unless the lesion fails to respond to treatment or recurs, the patient is older, or the mass is hard or irregular. C
Antibiotics, if prescribed, should be chosen to treat possible sexually transmitted infection (STI). C
Simple, small cysts can be managed with watchful waiting or sitz baths while incision and drainage combined with a drainage procedure are recommended for larger, more painful abscesses. B
In older patients with an irregular mass, suspect cancer. C

background.definition: The Bartholin's glands (also called greater or major vestibular glands) are 2 mucus-secreting pea-sized glands of the female genitalia that are situated in the base of the labia minora at the posterolateral aspect of the vestibule (at 4 O'clock and 8 O'clock positions). They are homologous to the bulbourethral glands (Cowper's) in the male. The mucus secreted by the Bartholin glands drains to the surface of the vagina, facilitating sexual function and providing moisture for the vestibular surface of the vagina. If the secretory duct of a Bartholin's gland becomes obstructed, secretions collect to form a cyst (Bartholin cyst). Bartholin cysts may appear after trauma of the area, pregnancy, episiotomy and unknown causes. When the cyst is infected, it is called Bartholin abscess (BA) or bartholinitis.

list.listitem: The lifetime incidence of BA is about 2%.
Patients more often present with BA than with simple Bartholin cyst (82% vs. 18%).
BA is more common prior to age 30 years, likely because of spontaneous involution of Bartholin's glands after age 30 years.

BA can occur during pregnancy, especially in the 2nd and 3rd timester. In one retrospective French study conducted in a university center from 2005-2015, 40 of 156 women who underwent surgical treatment for Bartholin abscess were pregnant; the incidence rate for pregnant women was 0.13%.
Usually polymicrobial, including both anaerobic (most common) and aerobic organisms.

Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, Gardnerella vaginalis, Proteus mirabilis, Pseudomonas, and anaerobic organisms are all commonly implicated as infectious agents in BA.

In one retrospective study, a majority of isolated infections from BA were caused by opportunistic organisms (as single or multiple). Coliforms and anaerobes were the most common bacteria in this series. The organisms causing BA vary with the population studied.

In an Israeli case series of 219 women admitted with BA, pus cultures were positive in 126 (61.8%) cases. Escherichia coli was the most frequent pathogen (43.7%) and was more common in recurrent vs. primary infections (56.8% vs. 37%, respectively). Ten cases (7.9%) were polymicrobial.

In a retrospective study of 75,000 Emergency Department patients, 64 patients had a diagnosis of Bartholin cyst or abscess and 40 of them also tested positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis.

The presence of altered anatomy (eg, postsurgical changes from vulvovaginal surgery, episiotomy) may contribute to Bartholin cysts and BA due to mechanical obstruction or damage to the Bartholin gland duct.
Bartholin's gland cyst in a neonate can be associated with hydrouretero-nephrosis and contralateral renal cyst that may cause urinary retention.
Bartholin abscess and cyst are more common in nonwhite patients, younger women and pregnant women and are less common with increasing parity (see ).

Bartholin's glands consist of lobules of acinar epithelium, draining into secondary ductules, which in turn drain into the vestibule (groove between the hymen and the labia minora) through the 2.0- to 2.5-cm-long Bartholin duct.

The glands are small (<1 cm; pea-sized) and normally not palpable. However, obstruction of the Bartholin duct sometimes leads to collected secretions that ultimately form a Bartholin's gland cyst. Such cysts vary in size from just over 1 cm to 5-10 cm or greater. When Bartholin's gland secretions become infected, an abscess (BA) may form. Perhaps counterintuitively, a BA typically involves the duct of the gland, rather than the gland itself.
Rarely, malignancy can induce changes appearing physically similar to a BA, especially in older patients.
Patients typically present with a soft, painful, fluctuant lump 1 to 3 cm in diameter on either side of the labia. C
Culture of abscess fluid is recommended, but biopsy or imaging is not recommended unless the lesion fails to respond to treatment or recurs. C

list.listitem: BA can be exquisitely tender or even painful at rest. If not infected, women may present with an asymptomatic mass that is brought to medical attention simply for cosmetic reasons or may be discovered during routine examination.

The onset of symptoms with abscess may be rapid over a matter of days or even hours. The patient may give a history of unilateral (rarely bilateral) labial edema and later swelling associated with pain, superficial dyspareunia, and sometimes difficulty in sitting or walking and fever. If the abscess bursts spontaneously, there is sudden relief of symptoms. Some patients may present to the examination room with a broad-based gait due to the swelling and pain.

Clinical examination may reveal a palpable mass (a normal Bartholin gland is not palpable). The swelling may be a soft, painful, fluctuant lump 1 to 10 cm in diameter on either side of the labia minora. Larger abscess may present as shiny midlabial swelling. Local examination may reveal enlarged, palpable, and tender inguinal nodes on the ipsilateral side of the abscess.
Abscess secretions should be cultured for aerobic and anaerobic organisms.
Also test for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis using a nucleic acid hybridization test (NAAT) or culture.
If the diagnosis is uncertain, ultrasound, CT, or MRI can be helpful. CT or MRI can be done when malignancy with possible invasion is suspected.
Biopsy lesions that fail to respond rapidly to standard interventions. Also, biopsy recurrent lesions to rule out cancer, especially in women older than 40 years.
BA is usually a clinical diagnosis, but in cases when there is uncertainty, ultrasound, CT, or MRI scan can be helpful.
The abscess secretions should be cultured and testing for STIs considered.
Lesions that fail to respond to standard interventions or recurrent lesions should be biopsied to rule out cancer, especially in women older than 40 years.
Consider drainage and biopsy of Bartholin cyst on women over 40 years of age.
Simple, small Bartholin cysts can be managed with watchful waiting, and small and less painful BAs can be managed with sitz baths and conservative measures. C

Incision and drainage (I&D) of the abscess combined with a drainage procedure (Word catheter placement or marsupialization, or fistulization using Foley catheter or Jacobi ring) results in fewer recurrences. A Alternative procedures include abolition of the gland (sclerotherapy, silver nitrate gland ablation, laser, or excision). B
If STI is suspected as the etiology for the BA, appropriate antibiotics should be administered while waiting for culture or NAAT results. A
Patients with simple Bartholin cyst do not require antibiotic therapy.
Antibiotics are commonly used for BA, even though drainage of the infected area may be adequate.

Standard therapy for chlamydia and gonorrhea are appropriate when these are clinically suspected pending culture or NAAT testing. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2015)-approved regimens include azithromycin 1 g single dose for chlamydia and ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular single dose for gonorrhea.

Other regimens are also acceptable, but a pregnancy test is recommended before initiation of treatment. These regimens include: (1) doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 to 10 days (contraindicated in children and pregnant women) and (2) cefixime 800 mg by mouth (to cover E. coli and N. gonorrhoeae) and clindamycin 300 mg by mouth 4 times daily for 5 to 7 days.

There are a variety of surgical approaches to BA, ranging from simple I&D to laser treatment (). In simple BA, Word catheter placement after drainage of the abscess is the preferred method. All interventions have potential limitations, and recurrences may be seen (0%-75% of cases). There are few randomized trials and a systematic review failed to identify a best approach.
Authors of a systematic review of treatments for BA from 8 trials with 699 women were unable to find evidence supporting any particular intervention over another.

In an RCT of 154 women with a first BA randomized to either marsupialization or gland excision, 5 women had recurrence following marsupialization vs. none from the excision group; more women had dyspareunia after marsupialization (15.1% vs. 2.9%, respectively). Sexual function improved in both groups.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence endorses use of balloon catheter insertion based on case series demonstrating high rates of abscess resolution in nearly all women. In the largest case series of 46 women, recurrence rates were reported in 17%. Adverse effects include mild-moderate discomfort and rarley necrotic abscess development.

I&D of the abscess combined with a drainage procedure (Word catheter placement, Jacobi ring or marsupialization) appears to result in fewer recurrences. Alternative procedures include abolition of the gland (sclerotherapy or excision).

In a French economic analysis, using 2016 data for the 3539 women who were hospitalized and underwent 3646 incisions of BA, 11.4% underwent at least one new Bartholin's gland procedure during the following year. Investigators estimated that use of the Word catheter in the outpatient setting would allow potential savings over 5 years of €7.4 million.
In a case series of 147 women with BA who received CO2 laser therapy, median operative time was 15 minutes (range, 12-35 minutes) and relapse rate at 3 years was 11.4% at 3 years.
In cases of recurrence, marsupialization is the treatment of choice, and in selected cases excision can be performed.
Sitz bath and warm soaking can be used to reduce symptoms or during the postoperative period, but no clinical trials are available on their efficacy.
Watchful waiting is appropriate for small, asymptomatic Bartholin cysts.
Recurrence is common following I&D.
Patients can rarely develop serious complications such as gangrene, necrotizing fasciitis, toxic shock syndrome, and septic shock that may require hospitalization.
Suspect cancer in the older patient with vulvar mass.
Diagnosis is made with history and focused clinical examination.
Small cysts do not require any surgical procedures during pregnancy. Infected cysts and large cysts should be managed with I&D or Word catheter.
BA in pregnancy requires antibiotic administration (see contraindication in pregnancy).
